description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: Fiction Is the Strongest Force in History
cards.subtitle: You'll never meet the 200,000 people who work for your company. Yet you all show up for the same imaginary thing.
body: Chimpanzees can't coordinate past 150 individuals. Humans built cities of millions by inventing shared stories—gods, nations, corporations, human rights.
The story doesn't need to be true. It needs to be believed by strangers simultaneously.
cards.takeaway: Shared myths are the technology that scales human collaboration.

cards.title: The Agricultural Revolution Was a Trap
cards.subtitle: Your ancestors worked 20 hours a week foraging. Then they planted wheat. Now they work dawn to dusk and their backs hurt.
body: Hunter-gatherers ate dozens of food sources and moved when resources ran low. Farmers bet everything on one crop.

• The species exploded in numbers
• Individual lives got shorter, sicker, harder
• Once population grew, there was no way back
cards.takeaway: Wheat spread across continents. Humans became its distribution system.

cards.title: Gossip Built Civilization
cards.subtitle: You trust the new trader because someone you trust said he's honest. You've never met him. That's the entire trick.
body: Language didn't evolve for hunting plans or tool instructions. It evolved to track who's reliable, who cheats, who's sleeping with whom.
Social information scaled trust beyond personal relationships. Reputation traveled faster than people did.
cards.takeaway: Gossip was the first distributed database of human behavior.

cards.title: Strangers Cooperate Because of Shared Myths
cards.subtitle: Two lawyers from different continents close a deal in twenty minutes. They've never met. They both believe in contracts.
body: You hand money to a stranger for a product you'll receive next week. This works because you both believe in payment systems, legal enforcement, and property rights.
The fiction isn't a lie—it's an agreement. It exists because enough people act like it does.
cards.takeaway: Coordination at scale requires shared belief in imaginary things.

cards.title: Money and Credit Are Belief Systems
cards.subtitle: You trade forty hours of your life for numbers in a database. A bank lends money it doesn't have. Both work because everyone believes.
body: A dollar bill is cotton and ink. A bank balance is electricity arranged in patterns. None of these have intrinsic value.

• Credit didn't exist in pre-modern economies—they assumed a fixed pie
• Capitalism assumes infinite growth
• Credit is monetized belief in a future that doesn't exist yet
cards.takeaway: The second mass belief breaks, the paper is just paper.

cards.title: Empires Spread by Absorbing, Not Destroying
cards.subtitle: Rome conquers your city. Then it offers you roads, citizenship, and their gods. Three generations later, your grandson fights for Rome.
body: Burning cities is expensive. Occupying them forever is exhausting. Rome offered the conquered a deal: adopt our language, use our law, worship our gods.
Cultural absorption is cheaper than military control and lasts longer. Latin outlived the empire by a thousand years.
cards.takeaway: Hybrid cultures are more durable than pure ones enforced by force.

cards.title: Science Began With Admitting Ignorance
cards.subtitle: The priest says he knows why the crops failed. The scientist says she doesn't know yet. Guess which one builds an irrigation system.
body: Before modern science, knowledge systems claimed completeness. The Bible explained everything. So did the Quran, so did Confucius.
Science started by saying 'we don't know'. Then it built a method to reduce ignorance systematically.
cards.takeaway: Progress requires acknowledging what you don't yet understand.

cards.title: Biology Allows, Culture Decides
cards.subtitle: Someone tells you women can't lead because it's biology. Then you find a dozen societies where they always have.
body: Gender roles, family structures, sexual norms—they feel hardwired. Then you read about another culture that does the exact opposite.
Nature determines what's possible. Culture determines what's permitted. 'Unnatural' usually means 'uncommon here recently.'
cards.takeaway: Biology is permissive; culture is selective.

cards.title: Happiness Didn't Scale With Progress
cards.subtitle: You have antibiotics, air conditioning, and unlimited entertainment. The medieval peasant had none of those. You're both equally stressed.
body: Progress raised material conditions dramatically. Happiness seems roughly flat. Well-being tracks expectations and social bonds more than comfort.
The peasant had community and no comparison points. You have options and constant benchmarking.
cards.takeaway: Happiness is relative to what you expect, not what you have.

cards.title: Writing Was Invented for Taxes, Not Poetry
cards.subtitle: The first sentence ever written wasn't philosophy. It was '5 bushels of barley owed by Kushim.'
body: Writing emerged in Sumer around 3,000 BC because grain stores got too large to remember. Debts, property, taxes—bureaucracy forced record-keeping.
Poetry came a thousand years later. Surplus creates complexity; complexity demands documentation.
cards.takeaway: Every transformative cultural tool starts with a boring logistical problem.

cards.title: Wheat Domesticated Humans
cards.subtitle: You spend all day clearing rocks, hauling water, and pulling weeds. The wheat is thriving. Your back is ruined.
body: Humans settled in one place, cleared forests, and devoted their lives to a single plant's reproductive cycle.

• Wheat spread across continents
• Individual human lives got harder, shorter, sicker
• Humans traded mobility and variety for dependence on one crop
cards.takeaway: From the plant's perspective, agriculture was a massive win.

cards.title: There Were Other Human Species
cards.subtitle: Neanderthals were here for 300,000 years. Homo sapiens showed up. Within 10,000 years, Neanderthals were gone.
body: The planet had Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo erectus, Homo floresiensis—all human, none of them us. Then sapiens spread out of Africa.
We carry 2% Neanderthal DNA, so some mixing happened. Then they vanished.
cards.takeaway: Our uniqueness isn't inherent—it's the result of everyone else disappearing.

cards.title: Religion Is a Contract With the Invisible
cards.subtitle: You don't eat pork. Neither does the stranger. You both follow the same invisible rules. Now you can do business.
body: Polytheism, monotheism, Buddhism—each is a deal with forces you can't see. Follow these rules, get rewards you can't measure.
The deals didn't work because the gods were real. They worked because millions of believers coordinated their behavior.
cards.takeaway: The practical power of belief is independent of its truth.

cards.title: The Cognitive Revolution Made Us Different
cards.subtitle: 70,000 years ago something changed in the sapiens brain. We started telling stories. Then we conquered the planet.
body: For 2 million years humans existed without dominating. Then Homo sapiens developed the ability to talk about things that don't exist.
We didn't get smarter about rocks and plants. We got better at coordinating around collective fictions.
cards.takeaway: Language sophisticated enough to create shared myths made us unstoppable.

cards.title: The Individual Is a Recent Invention
cards.subtitle: Your great-great-grandfather didn't ask what he wanted to be. He was a Miller. His father was a Miller. So was his son.
body: For 95% of human history, identity came from lineage. You were your family, your village, your guild.

• The idea that you have personal rights is shockingly recent
• Communities, not individuals, were the unit of society
• Modern loneliness is the cost of individualism
cards.takeaway: Personal identity as we know it is a modern experiment.

cards.title: Technology Is What Makes Us Human
cards.subtitle: Every species has biology. Only humans have nuclear reactors, vaccines, and space telescopes.
body: Biology gave us opposable thumbs and big brains. Technology is what we did with them. Fire let us cook food and gain calories that fueled bigger brains.
A chimpanzee today is as capable as a chimpanzee 100,000 years ago. A human today carries the accumulated technology of millennia.
cards.takeaway: Technology isn't separate from being human—it's the defining trait.

cards.title: Justice Is a Story Groups Agree On
cards.subtitle: You say everyone has rights. Someone asks you to show them the 'equality molecule.' You can't. It's a story. It works anyway.
body: Human rights have no biological foundation. There's no liberty gene or justice particle. Rights exist because groups wrote them into shared stories.
Justice is an imagined order, not a natural law. This doesn't make rights less valuable—it makes them more fragile.
cards.takeaway: The stories we believe together shape what's possible.

cards.title: War Declined Because It Stopped Paying
cards.subtitle: You invade Silicon Valley. You seize the office buildings. The engineers leave. You now own empty offices and worthless servers.
body: In an agricultural economy, you could seize a wheat field and immediately profit. In a knowledge economy, wealth is in people's heads.
You can't loot intellectual property or kidnap human capital at scale. Conquest stopped making economic sense.
cards.takeaway: Peace is partly maintained by economics, not just morality.

cards.title: We Are the Most Dangerous Animal That Ever Lived
cards.subtitle: Humans arrive in Australia 50,000 years ago. Within 2,000 years, 90% of large animals are extinct.
body: Everywhere sapiens migrated—Australia, the Americas, Pacific islands—megafauna disappeared within centuries.

• Giant sloths, woolly mammoths, cave lions—we showed up, they vanished
• The correlation is overwhelming
• No asteroid required
cards.takeaway: Ecological destruction isn't a modern problem—it's a species trait.

cards.title: No One Chose This Future
cards.subtitle: Your ancestor planted extra wheat to feed his family. Now his descendant works in a cubicle and pays taxes. Nobody planned that.
body: The agricultural revolution wasn't a decision anyone made. Neither was capitalism, the nation-state, or the internet. Each step felt local and logical.
Small choices compound into massive unintended outcomes. The gap between intention and result is where history happens.
cards.takeaway: The aggregate result is a world nobody designed and nobody controls.
